title: China’s ICE Sales Plummet 49% as EVs Surge to 67% Share in September Report
body:
China’s automotive market delivered a stark signal this September: sales of conventional internal‑combustion‑engine (ICE) vehicles plummeted nearly half, while electric cars surged to dominate two‑thirds of all new registrations. The China Association of Automobile Manufacturers (CAAM) reported a 49 % year‑on‑year drop in ICE sales, contrasted with a 67 % market share for battery‑electric vehicles (BEVs) and plug‑in hybrids combined. The shift underscores the rapid pace of China’s electrification drive and hints at a restructuring of the global auto industry that could reverberate far beyond the nation’s borders.

The numbers are striking. In September, total passenger‑vehicle sales fell 3.9 % from the same month a year earlier, but the decline was driven almost entirely by gasoline and diesel models, which slid from 2.3 million units in September 2023 to just 1.2 million in September 2024. By contrast, electric vehicle registrations climbed to 1.5 million, up from 0.9 million a year earlier. The EV surge was powered by both pure‑battery models and plug‑in hybrids, with domestic manufacturers accounting for roughly 80 % of the growth. Brands such as BYD, SAIC‑Volkswagen, and Changan led the charge, while foreign incumbents like Tesla and Volkswagen continued to expand capacity in Shanghai and Wuhan.

Analysts attribute the plunge in ICE demand to a confluence of policy, pricing and consumer sentiment. Since early 2024, the Chinese government has tightened subsidies for fossil‑fuel cars while extending generous incentives for EV buyers, including tax exemptions, license‑plate lotteries and lower down‑payment requirements. Simultaneously, stricter emissions standards and the gradual phasing out of low‑efficiency models have squeezed the profitability of ICE production lines. On the demand side, Chinese consumers—particularly younger urban buyers—are increasingly prioritising low operating costs, smart‑connected features and the prestige of owning a zero‑emission vehicle. The result is a market where the average new‑car buyer is now more likely to opt for an electric powertrain than a traditional gasoline engine.

The ripple effects are already being felt across the supply chain. Traditional component makers that specialise in exhaust systems, fuel pumps and transmission gearboxes are scrambling to diversify into electric‑driven parts such as inverters, battery management systems and high‑voltage cabling. Meanwhile, battery manufacturers are racing to secure raw‑material contracts and scale up gigafactory output to meet the heightened demand. The rapid adoption curve also raises questions about grid capacity, as the nation’s electricity infrastructure must accommodate an estimated additional 10 GWh of charging load per month if the current growth trajectory holds.

Internationally, China’s electrification surge could reshape global auto strategies. Many Western manufacturers have long relied on Chinese factories to achieve economies of scale for ICE models; the shift may compel them to retool plants for electric production or shift focus to other markets. Conversely, Chinese EV makers are gaining confidence to export more aggressively, with recent launches in Europe, Southeast Asia and South America. If the September trend continues, China could soon account for more than half of all global EV sales, reinforcing its position as the world’s foremost battery‑car hub.

Looking ahead, the momentum appears unlikely to stall. The Chinese government has signalled further tightening of ICE licensing in major megacities and is investing heavily in ultra‑fast charging networks, aiming for 1.5 million public chargers by 2027. Industry observers expect the ICE market share to dip below 30 % by the end of 2025, while EVs could capture upwards of 75 % of new car sales. The September data, therefore, is not an isolated spike but a clear inflection point that heralds a new era for mobility in the world’s largest auto market, with profound implications for manufacturers, suppliers and policymakers worldwide.
